Chapter 9: Designing for Diversity
The world isn’t made for just one kind of person, is it? What works beautifully for one of us—or even for one species—might not work at all for another. So, let’s take a look at what it really means to design environments, systems, and experiences that honor all the different ways we think, move, and feel.
Imagine a school principal walking down the hallway. She notices some kids are right at home in the bustling cafeteria, while others slip away to quiet corners. That’s when it hits her: this building was designed with the “average” student in mind. But honestly, is there really such a thing as average? Every child brings unique strengths, needs, and sensitivities to the table.
Here’s something to pay attention to—universal design. It’s all about creating spaces that feel accessible and comfortable for everyone, not just the majority. Think about it: on a farm, that means having plenty of shade, shelter, and different options for social interaction. And in schools or workplaces, it might look like quiet rooms, flexible schedules, or materials that aren’t overwhelming to the senses.
The story circles back to a woman in a cattle yard, experimenting with new layouts and materials. She tries curved chutes, solid walls, and non-slip floors. Suddenly, the animals move with ease—there’s less stress, and injuries drop. These changes aren’t complicated, but their impact is huge.
For people with autism, even the smallest adjustments can make a world of difference. Imagine dimming harsh lights, lowering the noise, or setting up clear routines. What was once overwhelming now feels inviting. And here’s the real point: these tweaks aren’t just special favors—they’re proof of respect for human diversity.
Let’s think even bigger. When we build systems for the so-called “average,” we end up leaving out anyone who doesn’t fit that mold. But if we design for those on the margins, we end up creating spaces that work better for everyone. It’s not just about being fair—designing this way sparks creativity and leads to new ideas.
So, what’s the key takeaway as we wrap up this chapter? True inclusion isn’t about asking people to change so they can fit in. It’s about reshaping the world so it fits all of us. That’s the heart of universal design—and the real challenge for anyone who cares about justice and equity.
